\chapter{Green and Yellow}
\label{ch:ml-green-and-yellow}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name green and yellow in Malayalam and say why the two come from unrelated roots.}

Say paccha beside Tamil paccai and mañña beside mañcaḷ, and show they are not doublets of each other.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\ml{പച്ച}, \ml{മഞ്ഞ}]{\ml{പച്ച}, \ml{മഞ്ഞ} — matching Tamil twice over, by two different routes}

\label{lesson:ML-C22-paccha-manja}



\begin{quote}
Telugu's green and yellow turned out to be one word wearing two faces. Malayalam's green and yellow are a different story again — two completely separate native words, each one matching Tamil closely, just not matching \emph{each other}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\ml{പച്ച}} (\textbf{paccha}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{green}\textquotedblright{}) comes from \textbf{Proto-Dravidian} \emph{\textbf{*pac-}} — matching \textbf{Tamil}'s \textbf{\ta{பச்சை}} (\emph{paccai}) almost exactly, and the same root already seen in Kannada's \emph{hasiru} and Telugu's \emph{pacca}. No surprises here; this is the familiar family from the last two lessons.

\begin{culture}
\textbf{\ml{മഞ്ഞ}} (\emph{mañña}, \textquotedblleft{}yellow\textquotedblright{}) and \textbf{\ml{മഞ്ഞൾ}} (\emph{maññaḷ}, \textquotedblleft{}turmeric\textquotedblright{}) are a native \textbf{doublet pair}. This is a \textbf{completely different} Dravidian root from \emph{pac-}, matching \textbf{Tamil}'s own turmeric/yellow pair, \textbf{\ta{மஞ்சள்}} (\emph{mañcaḷ}), closely. So here's the honest shape of this arc so far: Kannada split green and yellow into two unrelated families (native vs. Sanskrit loan); Telugu kept them as doublets of the \textbf{same} native root; and Malayalam keeps them as \textbf{two separate} native Dravidian roots, each one independently matching its Tamil counterpart. No single pattern holds across all three languages — the honest answer is that each solved \textquotedblleft{}green vs. yellow\textquotedblright{} its own way.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\ml{പച്ച}\textquotedblright{} — green, matching Tamil paccai
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\ml{മഞ്ഞ}\textquotedblright{} — yellow, matching Tamil mañcaḷ, a separate root entirely
  \item the contrast — paccha and mañña are NOT doublets of each other, unlike Telugu's pacca/pasupu
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Does \textbf{\ml{മഞ്ഞ}} (\emph{mañña}, \textquotedblleft{}yellow\textquotedblright{}) share a root with \textbf{\ml{പച്ച}} (\emph{paccha}, \textquotedblleft{}green\textquotedblright{})? (\textbf{No} — they are two separate native Dravidian roots.) What Tamil word does \textbf{\ml{മഞ്ഞ}} closely match? (\textbf{\ta{மஞ்சள்}}, \emph{mañcaḷ}, \textquotedblleft{}turmeric/yellow.\textquotedblright{}) Across Kannada, Telugu, and Malayalam, is there one single pattern for how green and yellow relate? (\textbf{No} — Kannada split them into native vs. Sanskrit-loan; Telugu made them doublets of one root; Malayalam keeps them as two separate native roots.)
\end{tcolorbox}
